content.p: Public Enemy Number 1 is a white supremacist gang that began in Southern California among teenagers who liked punk rock, and grew into a prison-and-street gang that the ADL and police describe as heavily involved in the drug trade and identity theft. Its members are often called PENI or PEN1. The ADL says members have been convicted of assault, attempted murder and murder. The gang's name echoes the phrase "public enemy No. 1", which Deseret News traces to the 1930s, when it was applied to the most wanted criminal of the day.

The Anti-Defamation League says the group was formed by white youths active in the punk music subculture of Southern California in the mid-1980s. NBC News, citing police, gives a similar start: a group of teenage punk-rock fans from upper-middle-class communities who began in Long Beach and later moved their base to nearby Orange County. In the 1990s, police told NBC, the gang began recruiting what they called "bored latchkey kids", white teenagers from comfortable neighbourhoods.

According to the ADL, the group soon split into two camps, one that stressed white supremacist ideology and another that concentrated on crime. The current leadership steered it toward criminal operations inside and outside prison. White males make up most of the membership, with women mostly in support roles, the ADL says.

The gang's growth is tied to changes inside California's prisons. The Aryan Brotherhood had long dominated white supremacist prison gangs, and the Nazi Low Riders acted as its foot soldiers on the outside. According to NBC News, officials in 2000 treated the Low Riders as a prison gang and put newly jailed members straight into solitary. The ADL dates the state's recognition of the Low Riders as a prison gang to 1999. NBC says the crackdown hurt the Low Riders' ability to deal with the Brotherhood, which then turned to Public Enemy.

The alliance was cemented in 2005, according to NBC, when Donald Reed "Popeye" Mazza, whom NBC calls a suspected leader of Public Enemy, joined the Brotherhood's ranks. The ADL describes Mazza as the group's "shot-caller" and says he had a violent history, including a 2003 conviction for attempted murder for which he was serving 15 years in a state prison. Under California's prison gang rules, the ADL notes, Public Enemy is not classed as a prison gang in the same way as the Brotherhood, and some of its leaders were placed in segregation as associates of a prison gang.

The ADL also reports a 1999 stabbing in which, according to prosecutors, a member was attacked in what the ADL calls a "prison-ordered hit", because fellow members suspected he was an informant for the police. Prosecutors think an Aryan Brotherhood member oversaw the attack. These are prosecutors' accounts as the ADL reports them, not findings of a court in the ADL text.

By 2007, according to NBC News, the gang's business also included white-collar crime alongside drugs. The ADL says members are heavily involved in the drug trade and also commit fraud, counterfeiting and identity theft. NBC News quotes Cpl. Nate Booth of the Buena Park police gang unit as saying the gang had gone from taking personal information from mailboxes and trash to stealing whole credit profiles, with help from girlfriends and wives who worked at banks, mortgage companies and state motor vehicle departments. Booth told NBC that the money from these schemes fed the gang's methamphetamine business.

Authorities also worried that the gang was using stolen credit information to find the home addresses of officers and their families, according to Booth, and that some officers had gone to court to have their addresses removed from records.

The ADL describes assaults, attempted murders and murders attributed to members in both prisons and streets. It also says members can be hard to count, because many also belong to other white racist gangs, which makes it difficult for police to measure the group's size or attribute crimes.

Estimates of membership vary by source and by year. The ADL reports that law enforcement put the membership at about 200 in 2003. By 2005, prison officials had documented 350 to 400 members, and the ADL says the total including associates could be as much as twice that, since many members are unknown to authorities. The ADL also cites California Department of Justice figures of about 300 documented members operating in northern and southern California, concentrated in Orange County and the Inland Empire.

NBC News, reporting in March 2007, said the ranks had doubled in the previous three years to at least 400, while authorities suspected hundreds more operated out of sight. The same report says recruiting was taking place in California and Arizona, and that members had been picked up in Nevada and Idaho. A probation official quoted by NBC summed up the problem: "They move around. We find them everywhere."

The figures do not agree, and the reports cover different years. The ADL's own profile notes that it is an archived report that may not reflect current facts, so none of these numbers should be read as today's membership.
content.h2: The December 2006 sweep and the hit list
content.p: In November 2006, authorities learned of an alleged "hit list" that named an Orange County prosecutor and five police officers in several departments. NBC News reported that the list targeted officers in Anaheim, Buena Park and Costa Mesa. The ADL says the Anaheim Police Department had already led a 10-month investigation into the gang before the list came to light.

On December 14, 2006, according to the ADL, nearly 300 officers from more than two dozen federal and local agencies carried out search and arrest warrants at some 75 locations across Southern California. The ADL reports 67 alleged members were arrested. The suspects were accused of plotting murder, holding illegal weapons and drugs, forgery, breaking probation and identity theft. NBC News, writing about two months later, said police had not released the names of those arrested or further details, because the investigation was continuing.
Neither source reports how those 2006 charges ended.

The best-documented killing in the ADL's pages is that of Scott Miller, described as a founding member of the gang. On March 8, 2002, Miller's body was discovered in an Anaheim alley, with a bullet wound to the back of his head fired from close range. Witnesses at the later trial testified that Billy Joe Johnson brought Miller to the alley, saying they were there for a drug deal, and that fellow members Michael Lamb and Jacob Rump were waiting there, according to the ADL's account of the 2009 trial.

The ADL reports that a year before the killing, Miller had appeared in a local television interview about the gang, including its drug trafficking. The station altered his voice and showed him only in silhouette, but some of his tattoos were visible. The ADL says the killing was retaliation for that interview. That motive is the ADL's reading of the case; the ADL does not say a court ruled on it.

Several days after the body was found, Lamb and Rump shot at an Anaheim police officer during a chase, according to the ADL. Both were later convicted of attempted murder of a police officer. The ADL says ballistic tests showed the gun used against the officer was the same one that killed Miller.

Lamb and Rump were tried together in a six-week trial in Orange County Superior Court. The ADL reports that a jury found them guilty on July 10, 2007, of first-degree murder and conspiracy, along with a killing carried out to benefit a street gang. The jury found that Lamb fired the fatal shot, which made him eligible for a death sentence. According to the ADL, a jury returned a death sentence on June 11, 2008, and a judge affirmed it on August 22, 2008.

A judge gave Rump a no-parole life term on October 5, 2007, the ADL says, and additional life terms and a further 83 years to life for other charges. Both men were also convicted of attempted murder of a police officer, street terrorism and firearms possession.

A third man, Billy Joe Johnson, was a former member who testified for the defence that he, not Lamb and Rump, had shot Miller. He said he had given Lamb the gun the next day. Under cross-examination, the ADL reports, he could not correctly describe the firearm, despite saying he had owned it for six months. Johnson was already serving 45 years to life for a 2004 hammer killing in Huntington Beach. On September 14, 2009, a jury in Orange County found him guilty of conspiracy to commit murder and first-degree murder, with enhancements for lying in wait and for the benefit of the gang. On October 29, 2009, a jury in Orange County recommended the death penalty. The ADL's 2009 article does not report a final sentence for Johnson.

OC Weekly, reporting on a grand jury indictment, described Joseph Govey as a member of the Public Enemy Number One Death Squad. He was charged with seven felonies, including possession of a firearm by a felon, reckless evasion of police, street terrorism, possession of a forged document, solicitation to commit murder, participation in a criminal street gang and attempted murder. The charges concerned events beginning on August 16, 2011, and OC Weekly reported that prosecutors alleged he worked with fellow members to plot the murder of a Huntington Beach man. OC Weekly reported that Govey pleaded not guilty and was held at the Theo Lacy Jail. That report does not give an outcome.
content.h2: The name and the older phrase
content.p: The phrase "public enemy No. 1" was in use long before this gang. Deseret News explains that the Chicago Crime Commission published a list of "public enemies" in April 1930, with 28 names headed by Al Capone, and that by 1931 Capone had been called public enemy No. 1. A 1931 film starring James Cagney helped spread the term. The FBI, according to the same paper, never kept an official list of public enemies, but by 1934 it was using the phrase for John Dillinger. Deseret News adds that the phrase later became a general catchphrase, used for everything from wolves to inflation.

The ADL says the group's PENI name comes from the 1980s British punk band Rudimentary Peni, with no other connection between the band and the gang. None of the sources cited here says how the "Public Enemy Number 1" name was chosen, or whether it was taken from that history. What they do show is that the phrase has been used to describe a single figure of the underworld and, much later, a street and prison gang whose members have been charged with serious violence.

Several points remain open. The ADL's profile is an archived report that it says may be out of date, and the newest case described in these reports is the indictment of Govey, whose crimes are alleged to date from 2011. The ADL gives Lamb's age as 33 in one article and 34 in another, and its 2008 article gives the verdict date as July 10 while a later sentence in the same piece gives 2007. The membership estimates come from different years and agencies and do not add up to a single current figure. No final sentence for Johnson is reported in the ADL's 2009 article, and the outcomes of the 2006 arrests are not reported in the coverage cited here.

Taken together, these reports describe a gang that grew from a Southern California punk scene into a criminal network tied to the prisons, and a series of prosecutions in which some members were convicted of murder. They do not show the gang's size or activity today.
